Gift Growth Planner for Pi App

Pi (파이) is Hanwha Life's custodial investment app for Korean families who want to invest for their children through tax-exempt gifts. I reframed the team's public web Gift Simulator into Gift Growth Planner: an in-app planner that shows each family what they can give their child, who can give it, and when.

Context

Long-term investing has been gaining ground with the Korean public, and that includes parents who want to start early for their children. Korea's gift tax rules make this accessible as long as they are reported: every 10 years, a child can receive a set amount from family without any gift tax. Pi lets families invest those gifts in a custodial account and digitally report them to the tax office without leaving the app.

To promote Pi, the team had built a web Gift Simulator. Anyone could open it in a browser and see how quickly tax-exempt gifts could grow if they were invested for a child starting today for 30 years.

Problem

The team wanted to bring the Gift Simulator into the app. On paper that sounded like moving a feature from one screen to another. In practice, the feature had to change what it was for.

On the web, the simulator spoke to anyone who found it, with example numbers. Inside Pi, the app knows each child's real age and the gifts the user had already reported through HomeTax, Korea's online tax service.

The question the feature answered changed with it as it moved from the browser into the app:

Answering this question meant making sense of rules that most parents only discover after they've already made a gift:

My task was to bring this browser feature into the mobile app and turn these overlapping timelines with complex numbers into something a parent could easily follow on a phone, for their own child.

Research

To inform the design process and decisions, I requested information and materials on feedback the app had received previously. Through support tickets, user reviews, and usability test reviews from the QA engineers, we synthesized the findings through an affinity map to see what user needs this new feature could address.

Affinity map

I sorted what users said alongside the questions it raised for the product managers and me, and grouped them into four themes.

Personas

The web simulator only had to serve one kind of visitor: someone curious. The app had to serve families at very different points, so we built the planner around four of them.

Each persona ended up shaping a specific part of the design.

Process

User flow

The initial user flow was a general outline of how a user might move through the feature, and what value it could give them as an in-app feature. The row underneath maps what the family gets at each step.

First wireframes

The first wireframes were finance-style and close to the web version, with transparency as the first priority.

I first brainstormed ways to fit the planner into existing features, like showing it after a family invests. Feedback during the design process made me realize that a new feature inside an existing one could overcomplicate the process. That led me to make it a separate, new feature, designed as a planning experience of its own.

What the product managers said

  • It felt like a calculator.
  • It didn't really target the user feedback.
  • It didn't evolve from the original implementation.

Wireframes after feedback

I broke the flow down into smaller steps and put accessibility and enjoyability first. The transparency stayed the same, just broken down into related interactive sections rather than shown all at once.

I turned these into a lo-fi prototype and presented it to designers and product managers for another round of feedback before moving to the final design.

My biggest takeaway was not to be afraid to break a process down into smaller parts. Users will stick through it if it's enjoyable and accessible.

Solution

From a simulator to a planner, measured like a height chart

Parents already track how their children grow: pencil marks on a door frame, a height chart on the bedroom wall. I helped reframe the simulator around that same habit, showing how savings grow up alongside the child. The name changed with it, from Gift Simulator to Gift Growth Planner.

0 10 19 30 40
Age 0

A swipeable timeline, one stop per tax-exempt window

The web version borrowed from subway map UIs, with a vertical line of stops marking when each tax-exempt period renews from the child's age today to 30 years out.

In the app, the timeline turned horizontal and swipeable. Each stop is one 10-year window and shows the child's age, how much the family can still give, and the child at that age. The line changes color at 19, and where the adult allowance opens while the minor one is still running, a second line appears alongside it. That overlap is the rule families misunderstand most, so we chose to show it rather than explain it. Small tags on the line open short explanations for that stage, and the details of how much to give and who gives it sit behind the action buttons instead of crowding the timeline.

Built for one phone and one family

The web simulator had to work in any browser for anyone. In the app, we could design for a small screen and a specific child:

Outcome

A new conversation about usability

Leadership had mostly measured the app by usage and retention. Walking them through the planner with real family situations, like a grandparent who can't give because the parents already have, or twins who aren't born yet, shifted the conversation. Usability and personalization started being discussed as priorities for an app meant for very different families.

A reason to open the app between gifts

Before, Pi was somewhere you went to invest and report a gift. The planner gave families a reason to come back in between. Users told us they could see their plan, their remaining allowance, and their next window without working it out themselves outside the app. Parents who had given before joining Pi also found a use for it, as a planner for when their current tax-exempt window runs out.

Learning as a next step

The planner ended up teaching families how gifting rules and custodial investing work, almost as a side effect. That led the team to discuss building dedicated learning features alongside it.
